title: ETH hardness of constant-factor shortest-vector approximation for \(1\le p\le 2\)
formal: Does deterministic ETH imply that for every fixed real \(p\in [1,2]\) there is a constant \(\gamma >1\) for which the gap shortest-vector problem \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) has no deterministic algorithm running in time \(2^{o}(d)N^{O}(1)\), where d is the ambient lattice dimension and N is the explicit input bit length?
why: Would strengthen the fine-grained hardness basis for constant-factor lattice approximation in the most familiar norm range, using an ordinary satisfiability assumption. It separates a genuine exponential obstruction from lower bounds relying on a stronger gap or randomized premise.
status_note: Published source and definitions checked through 11 September 2026. Hair–Sahai’s 2026 deterministic hardness result was also checked: its subexponential reduction does not supply the displayed \(2^{o}(d)\) lower bound in output lattice dimension. No matching resolution of the ordinary-ETH target for \(1\le p\le 2\) was located.

progress.text: The paper establishes ordinary-ETH constant-gap CVP hardness and randomized-ETH SVP hardness for \(p>2\), while explicitly leaving \(p\in [1,2]\) open.

Hair and Sahai’s revised preprint gives deterministic hardness for all finite norms; its reduction-size regime is different from the dimension-linear fine-grained requirement here. The work is accepted at FOCS 2026.

sentences: The shortest-vector problem asks how short a nonzero lattice vector can be.
This card asks for constant-factor gap hardness in every norm \(\ell p\) with \(1\le p\le 2\).
The proposed lower bound excludes subexponential dependence on ambient dimension, with polynomial dependence on input encoding length.
Its premise is ordinary deterministic ETH, and the approximation factor must stay bounded away from one as dimension grows.
The source’s shortest-vector hardness theorem for \(p>2\) uses randomized ETH and does not settle this stated interval or premise.

references.title: Mind the Gap? Not for SVP Hardness Under ETH!
references.authors: Aggarwal, Divesh; Gupta, Rishav; Morolia, Aditya; Zhang, Chuanqi

definitions: An input consists of integers \(d\ge r\ge 1, a\) rational \(d\times r\) matrix B with linearly independent columns, and a positive rational threshold R. All rationals are given by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators with delimiters; N is the total bit length. The lattice is \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{r}\}\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{d}\). For fixed \(p\in [1,2]\), the norm is \(\Vert x\Vert _{p}=(\sum _{i=1}^{d}|x_{i}|^{p})^{1/p}\), and \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{p}:v\in \mathrm{L}, v\ne 0\}\). \(SVP_{p,\gamma}\) accepts if \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})\le R\) and rejects if \(\lambda _{1}^{p}(\mathrm{L})>\gamma R\). Inputs between these thresholds are outside the promise; either answer is permitted there. The requested task is gap decision, not output of a lattice vector. The norm parameter and gap are fixed mathematical constants, not part of the input, and one finite deterministic Turing-machine program must solve all promised inputs for them. A subexponential bound means time at most \(2^{h(d)}N^{c}\) for some fixed c and nonnegative h with \(h(d)/d\to 0\). Bounds and programs may depend on p and \(\gamma\). The dimension convention follows the source’s lower-bound statements for lattices in \(\mathbb{R} ^{d}\); rank \(r\le d\) is displayed separately. ETH here asserts that for some \(\delta >0\) there is no deterministic algorithm deciding 3-CNF satisfiability on v variables in \(O(2^{\delta v}M^{c})\) time for any fixed c, where M is the formula’s bit length. It is the ordinary satisfiability assumption, not a promise that unsatisfiable instances have a constant fraction of violated clauses. Randomized ETH instead excludes bounded-error randomized algorithms and is a different premise. The card follows the literal deterministic-ETH version of Open Problem 1.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the implication from ordinary deterministic ETH to the stated constant-gap subexponential lower bound for every fixed \(p\in [1,2]\). The constant \(\gamma\) may depend on p but must be strictly greater than one and independent of dimension. A result using GapETH, or only randomized ETH, does not by itself prove this precise implication.

context_blocks.title: The gap concerns the shortest nonzero vector
context_blocks.text: The zero vector belongs to every lattice and is excluded from the minimum. In \(\mathbb{Z} ^{2}\) the shortest nonzero vector has norm one for every p in this range. A YES instance has such a vector within radius R; a NO instance has none within the larger radius \(\gamma R\).

context_blocks.title: A constant approximation gap must survive dimension growth
context_blocks.text: The desired factor \(\gamma\) is fixed once the norm is chosen. A hardness result whose factor approaches one as dimension grows would not meet the question. Conversely, the target does not require hardness for every constant factor, only for some factor greater than one at each p.

context_blocks.title: The source distinguishes its assumptions
context_blocks.text: The paper proves ordinary-ETH hardness for constant-gap closest vector in all finite \(\ell p\) norms. Its shortest-vector result for \(p>2\) uses randomized ETH. Closest vector has a specified target point, while shortest vector looks for a short nonzero vector around the origin; the two tasks and the two ETH variants are kept separate.

context_blocks.title: The missing norm range includes Euclidean geometry
context_blocks.text: At \(p=1\) the norm sums absolute coordinates, while at \(p=2\) it is Euclidean length. The source leaves this whole interval as an open shortest-vector hardness target. Its result outside the interval therefore does not establish the displayed claim.

context_blocks.title: A later deterministic breakthrough has different size guarantees
context_blocks.text: Hair and Sahai give deterministic hardness of approximation in every finite \(\ell p\) norm, including \(p=2\), in a work accepted at FOCS 2026. Their reduction uses a subexponential-size/time regime relative to the SAT instance. This is substantial progress on removing randomization, but its stated hardness does not exclude every \(2^{o}(d)\)-time algorithm in the output lattice dimension, as this card requests.
